opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
## When You Don't Feel Like One of the Ninety-Nine

*Matthew 18:1–5, 10, 12–14*

In Matthew 18, Jesus places a child among His disciples and tells them that unless they turn and become like children, they will not enter the Kingdom of Heaven. He tells them not to despise these “little ones,” because their angels in heaven always look upon the face of the Father. Then He speaks of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine to search for the one who has gone astray.

There is something deeply comforting in the way these teachings belong together.
The child is not important because the child is accomplished, productive, dependable or useful. The child has done nothing to earn a place before God. Yet Jesus tells us that the angels of these little ones continually behold the face of His Father.
Their worth already exists.
As adults, we can lose sight of that.

Some of us learn to create our worth by becoming necessary. We work. We provide. We solve problems. We take care of people. We become the person everyone can rely upon. Sometimes, without even realizing it, being needed becomes a form of security.

If I am useful enough, perhaps I will always have a place.

If someone depends upon me, perhaps they will not leave.
If I can keep everything together, perhaps everything will remain together.
But eventually life can exhaust our ability to do that.
Responsibilities become heavier. Relationships change. Confidence disappears. Things we once controlled begin slipping beyond our control. And when our usefulness is no longer enough to make us feel secure, we are left facing a much more difficult question:

**Who am I when I am no longer proving my worth?**

This is where the child in Matthew 18 becomes so important.
Jesus does not tell us to become childish. He tells us to become like children. A child has little status, little power, and little ability to control the world around her. She receives. She trusts. She reaches for the person she believes will hold her.

Perhaps becoming like a child means surrendering the belief that we must earn our right to be loved.
And then there are the sheep.
There are times when I don't necessarily see myself as the lost sheep, but I don't feel as though I belong comfortably among the ninety-nine either.
I can look within myself and see things I don't like. Suspicion. Jealousy. Anger. Distrust. Fear of being alone. I can question relationships I thought were secure and wonder whether some of what I called strength was actually fear—the fear that if I stopped carrying everything, something important might fall apart.
Then comes the uncomfortable question:

**How can this person be among the ninety-nine?**

Perhaps because the ninety-nine were never ninety-nine perfect people.
Being among God's sheep does not mean we have conquered every weakness within ourselves. It does not mean we never become frightened, jealous, resentful, angry or uncertain.
We belong because we belong to the Shepherd.
And remarkably, the same is true of the one who wanders.
The shepherd does not search for the lost sheep because that sheep has demonstrated its usefulness. He searches because the sheep is his.

That changes everything.

At different times in life, any of us may become the one. We become exhausted, frightened, confused or separated from the life we once recognized. We may even become strangers to ourselves.
God does not stand among the ninety-nine waiting for us to prove that we deserve to return.
He comes looking.
Perhaps this is why Jesus first places a child before us.
Before the accomplishments, responsibilities, careers, marriages, possessions and identities we accumulate throughout adult life, there was simply the person God created.

The child.

Before she learned to prove herself.
Before she believed she had to be useful to be worthy.
Before she discovered how frightening loneliness could be.
Before she learned to make herself indispensable so that she might feel secure.
God already knew her.
And God already loved her.

Sometimes life strips away the things we have used to tell ourselves who we are. It can feel like everything is falling apart. But perhaps some of what is falling away was never our identity to begin with.
Our usefulness is not our identity.
Our fear is not our identity.
Our jealousy is not our identity.
Our relationships are not our identity.
Even our failures are not our identity.
At the center remains something much simpler:

**We are children of God.**

So perhaps the question is not whether I am worthy enough to stand among the ninety-nine.
Perhaps it is not even whether I have wandered far enough to become the one.
The Gospel gives the same answer to both.

**I belong to the Shepherd.**

And when everything else becomes uncertain, that may be the place from which life begins again.
